sections.html:
The Massachusetts homestead exemption protects equity in your primary home from most creditors, up to a set dollar amount. It is set out in G.L. c. 188 and comes in two forms: an automatic one and a declared one.

It is not a discount on the yearly property tax bill. Tax exemptions, deferrals and abatements are a separate matter handled through the local board of assessors. This page covers only the creditor protection under chapter 188.

The automatic exemption protects $125,000 of equity with no filing, and a recorded declaration raises the protection to $1,000,000. Both figures come from section 1 of the chapter.

Type of homesteadAmount protectedHow it arises
Automatic$125,000Exists for the owner and family who live in the home or intend to, with no filing (section 4)
Declared$1,000,000Created by a written declaration that is recorded (section 5)
Declared by an elderly or disabled ownerUp to $1,000,000 per personOwner is 62 or older, or disabled; a separate declaration under section 2

When a home is owned as joint tenants or tenants by the entirety, the exemption stays whole and unallocated, and the owners together cannot exceed the cap. Where owners are tenants in common or trust beneficiaries, the automatic exemption is divided by ownership share, and the declared exemption is divided among those who live in the home as a principal residence.

The statute defines a home broadly, so most owner-occupied residences qualify. A protected home can be any of these, along with the land and accessory structures that go with it:

  • A single-family house.
  • A two- to four-family dwelling.
  • A manufactured home.
  • A residential condominium unit.
  • A residential cooperative unit.

It must be a principal residence, meaning the place where the owner and family live or intend to live as their main dwelling. No person can hold rights in more than one principal residence. Family counts a spouse and any minor child, and the statute sets "minor child" at age 21 and under.

A federal bankruptcy court decision also found that using part of a property for business does not by itself remove homestead protection.

sections.h2: How to file a declaration of homestead
sections.html:
Sign a written declaration and record it at the Registry of Deeds for the county where the home sits. Section 5 sets what it must contain.

  • Each owner who is to benefit signs and acknowledges it under penalty of perjury.
  • It identifies each owner and any non-titled spouse.
  • It states that each person named lives in the home or intends to as a principal residence.
  • If a married couple co-owns the home as the principal residence of both, both spouses sign.
  • If the home is in a trust, only the trustee signs.
  • It cannot be created inside the deed that gives the owner title.
  • It should state whether anyone named may be a servicemember, though leaving that out does not void it.

The state filing fee is $35, and a county registry may add its own charge. The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds, for example, charges $36 for a declaration of homestead on recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost, and $35 on the Land Court side. You can file by mail with notarized signatures and a check.

sections.h2: Owners over 62 or with a disability
sections.html:
An elderly person is someone 62 or older. A disabled person is someone with a permanent impairment that would meet Supplemental Security Income standards. Either can record a separate declaration under section 2.

A disabled owner must record proof with the declaration: an original or certified Social Security Administration disability award letter, or a letter from a registered physician certifying that the federal standard is met. Each person benefited under section 2 gets the declared amount in full, without sharing it among other owners, and separate declarations under sections 2 and 3 can sit on the same home.

sections.h2: What happens to the homestead when you sell
sections.html:
A sale ends the homestead on the house but not the protection for the money. Section 10 lists nine ways a homestead terminates, and a deed is the most common one for sellers.

  • A deed to a non-family member, signed by the owner and by any non-owner spouse or former spouse who lives in the home.
  • A recorded release signed and acknowledged by the owner and that spouse.
  • Abandonment of the home as a principal residence, which ends the rights of the person who left.
  • A new declaration on a different property by the same owner.
  • A deed that states the grantor is unmarried or that the property is not the grantor's home.
  • A divorce judgment that requires conveying the home to the other spouse.

Under section 11, sale proceeds stay protected until you buy another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first. After fire or other casualty damage, protection lasts until repairs are done, another home is acquired, or two years pass, whichever comes first. Living in a trailer or other temporary housing does not count as establishing a principal residence.

Mortgages are treated separately from creditor claims. Section 8 of the chapter deals with prior mortgages and liens, and section 9 with subordination of the homestead to a mortgage signed by all owners. Section 10 adds that nothing in a mortgage or its documents ends a homestead, apart from that subordination. Section 4 allows the automatic exemption to be subordinated to a new loan or line of credit only if the loan is under $20,000, not secured by a recorded document, and signed by all record owners and non-titled spouses with a plain-language waiver.

You do not have to file a declaration again after refinancing, and both spouses may file. A 2021 Appeals Court decision allows a creditor to levy on an execution and then hold off collecting until the homestead lapses or the homeowner's equity exceeds the protected amount. So a judgment can still be waiting when a protected home is sold. Ask the title company or attorney what appears in the record.

sections.h2: What a seller should check before closing
sections.html:
Confirm whether a declaration is on record, and who signed it, before you accept a closing date. The Secretary of the Commonwealth keeps a list of registries you can use to look it up.

  • Search the property at the registry to see whether a declaration or release is recorded.
  • Find out whether a spouse or former spouse who lives in the home needs to sign the deed or a release.
  • Ask whether any judgment lien or tax lien must be paid at closing.
  • Keep proceeds in a way an attorney can explain, because section 11 protection ends one year after the sale unless a new home is bought sooner.

Homes held in trust or owned by several people can involve more signers, so have a real estate attorney read the paperwork first. If the house is going to a cash buyer, the same checks apply, and a clean search up front keeps the closing date from slipping.

faqs.a: Yes, to a degree. Chapter 188, section 4 gives an automatic exemption of $125,000 with no filing, as long as the owner and family live in the home or intend to. Recording a declaration raises the protected amount to $1,000,000.

faqs.q: Does the homestead exemption lower my property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. Chapter 188 protects home equity from creditors. Property tax exemptions and abatements are a separate topic handled by your local board of assessors.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to file a declaration of homestead?
faqs.a: The state fee is $35, and a registry may add its own charge. Norfolk County charges $36 for recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost.

faqs.q: Do I have to refile after refinancing?
faqs.a: No. There is no need to file the declaration again after a refinance.

faqs.q: What happens if I sell and buy another home?
faqs.a: Sale proceeds stay protected until you acquire another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first, under section 11.
